During the June to September period in 1985 and 1991, the Jocassee plant is expected to generate an average of 114,000 megawatt-hours per month, and 138,000 megawatt-hours per month respectively (Duke Power Company, 1976c). The corresponding water discharge during the period from the Jocassee Reservoir during the generating cycle would be about 1,505,000 acre-feet in 1985 and 1,822,000 acre-feet in 1991. This should eliminate all of the approximately 450,000 acre-feet of Jocassee optimum coldwater habitat in the main body of the lake.
The temperature of the top 160 feet of water in the Bad Creek upper reservoir when full would approximate the average temperature of the water pumped from the Jocassee Reservoir plus natural heating in the upper reservoir. In order to prevent withdrawal of water colder than 20°C from Jocassee Reservoir, Applicant proposes to construct a weir across the Whitewater River Cove about 1,600 feet downstream of the Bad Creek tailrace. The crest of the weir would be in the vicinity of the thermocline of the density gradient, about 40 to 50 feet below the normal water surface, of Lake Jocassee.
The total effectiveness of the proposed weir in preventing withdrawal of water below 20°C has not been fully demonstrated and it is expected that some colder water would contribute to the water being drawn from Lake Jocassee and the Whitewater River Cove epilimnion during the Bad Creek pumping cycle. The Bad Creek upper reservoir water would potentially be somewhat warmer than 20°C. This warmer water would be discharged into Jocassee Reservoir during the Bad Creek generating cycle.
For the period of June through September, the proposed Bad Creek project would discharge an estimated 553,000 acre-feet of water into Jocassee Reservoir. Assuming the Bad Creek Project withdraws 10 percent of its pumping water from the colder water layers in Jocassee Reservoir (i.e. water below 20°C) and the return flows are warmer than 20°C, the net replacement of water at a temperature below 20° C with water having a temperature above 20°C in Jocassee Reservoir would be about 35,000 acre-feet. If it is assumed that Bad Creek would withdraw 50 percent of its pumping water from the water layers in Jocassee having temperatures below 20°C, the net displacement of colder water with warmer water would be about 277,000 acre-feet. The percentage of Jocassee waters below 20°C, pumped into the upper Bad Creek Reservoir would be a function of the density gradient in Jocassee Reservoir and the effectiveness of the proposed weir in the Whitewater River arm.
